summary: Gives the theory behind SPKI certificates and access control lists, without technical detail about their structure. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary:
Most certificates answer the question who is this key. SPKI certificates answer a different question: is this key allowed to do this thing.

The RFC explains the ideas behind that, and then defines a way to compute an access decision from a pile of certificates, whatever format they happen to be in.

how does delegation work in spki
subtitle: The theory behind certificates whose job is to say what a key is allowed to do.

tldr.problem: Certificates are usually thought of as saying who a key belongs to, but what an application needs to know is whether the key is allowed to do something.
tldr.mechanism: SPKI certificates bind authorizations to keys, or to names that stand for keys, and can be delegated on. To compute an answer from certificates in any format, the RFC defines an intermediate form, the 5-tuple, and the rules for reducing two of them into one.
tldr.outcome: The document gives the theory rather than the wire format. It is Experimental and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Certificate format
facts.value: S-expressions with a defined canonical form

today: RFC 2693 is an Experimental document from September 1999 and has not been obsoleted. It gives the theory behind SPKI certificates and access control lists without going into the technical detail of the structures or their uses.

sections.title: What SPKI Certificates Are For
sections.content:
The SPKI Working Group developed a standard form for digital certificates whose main purpose is authorization rather than authentication. These structures bind either names or explicit authorizations to keys or other objects. The binding to a key can be directly to an explicit key, or indirectly through the hash of the key or a name for it. The name and authorization structures can be used separately or together. The RFC uses S-expressions as the standard format for these certificates and defines a canonical form for those S-expressions. As part of this development, a mechanism for deriving authorization decisions from a mixture of certificate types was developed and is presented in the document.

The document gives the theory behind SPKI certificates and ACLs without going into technical detail about those structures or their uses. Section 2 gives the history of name certification from 1976 onwards, section 3 discusses authorization rather than authentication as the desired purpose of a certificate, section 4 discusses delegation, section 5 discusses validity conditions, section 6 defines 5-tuples and their reduction, section 7 discusses key management, and section 8 the security considerations.

The glossary at the front of the document fixes the terms used throughout. An ACL is an access control list: a list of entries that anchors a certificate chain, sometimes called a list of root keys. The ACL is the source of empowerment for certificates: a certificate communicates power from its issuer to its subject, but the ACL is the source of that power, since it has the owner of the resource it controls as its implicit issuer. An ACL entry has potentially the same content as a certificate body, but has no issuer and is not signed, and there is most likely one ACL for each resource owner, if not for each controlled resource.

A CERTIFICATE is a signed instrument that empowers the subject. It contains at least an issuer and a subject, and can contain validity conditions, authorization and delegation information. Certificates come in three categories: ID, mapping a name to a key; Attribute, mapping an authorization to a name; and Authorization, mapping an authorization to a key. An SPKI authorization or attribute certificate can pass along all the empowerment it has received from the issuer, or it can pass along only a portion of that empowerment.

The ISSUER is the signer of a certificate and the source of empowerment that the certificate is communicating to the subject. The KEYHOLDER is the person or other entity that owns and controls a given private key. A PRINCIPAL is a cryptographic key capable of generating a digital signature; the document deals with public key signatures but any digital signature method should apply. A principal is said to speak by means of a digital signature, the statement made being the signed object, often a certificate, and the principal is said to speak for the keyholder. The SUBJECT is the thing empowered by a certificate or ACL entry, and can be a key, a name with the understanding that the name is mapped by certificate to some key or other object, a hash of some object, or a set of keys arranged in a threshold function. An S-EXPRESSION is the data format chosen for SPKI and SDSI: a LISP-like parenthesised expression with the limitations that empty lists are not allowed and the first element in any S-expression must be a string, called the type of the expression.
sections.plainLanguage: The document fixes a vocabulary first, because the same words are used in several different senses in the certificate world. A certificate has an issuer who signs it and a subject who is empowered by it, and it may or may not be allowed to pass its powers on.

sections.title: How Name Certification Got Here
sections.content:
Certificates were originally viewed as having one function: binding names to keys, or keys to names. The RFC traces this to the 1976 paper by Diffie and Hellman introducing public key cryptography, and notes that before that, key management was risky, involved and costly, sometimes employing special couriers with briefcases handcuffed to their wrists.

Diffie and Hellman's scheme placed the public key in a public directory along with the user's name and address, a modified telephone book that took the place of the trusted courier. Loren Kohnfelder, in a 1978 bachelor's thesis, noted that when reliable exchange of the encryption functions between communicants is impossible, the next best thing is to trust a third party, and introduced the Public File. In an effort to prevent performance problems, Kohnfelder invented a new construct: a digitally signed data record containing a name and a public key, which he called a CERTIFICATE. Because it was digitally signed, such a certificate could be held by untrusted parties and passed around from person to person, resolving the performance problems involved in a central directory.

Ten years later the ISO X.509 recommendation was published as part of X.500, which was to be a global, distributed database of named entities, a global on-line telephone book. X.509 certificates were defined to bind public keys to X.500 path names with the intention of noting which keyholder had permission to modify which directory nodes. The RFC is blunt about the likely outcome: the original X.500 plan is unlikely ever to come to fruition, since collections of directory entries are considered valuable or even confidential by their owners and are not likely to be released as a directory sub-tree, and the idea of a single globally unique name that everyone could use requires a single global naming discipline when there are already too many entities defining names outside one.

The Privacy Enhanced Mail effort adopted X.509 certificates with a different interpretation. Where X.509 originally meant that the keyholder may modify this portion of the X.500 database, PEM took the certificate to mean that the key speaks for the named person, turning an access control instrument into an identity instrument. The insistence on X.509 certificates with a single global root delayed PEM's adoption past its window of viability. At about the same time, in 1991, Phil Zimmermann's PGP was introduced with a different certificate model: instead of waiting for a single global root and a hierarchy of authorities descending from it, PGP allowed multiple, hopefully independent but not specially trusted individuals to sign a name and key association, with the theory that with enough such signatures the association could be trusted because not all those signers would be corrupt. This was the web of trust model.

Section 2.4 then rethinks the assumption that the job of a certificate is to bind a name to a key. Names are what people use as identifiers, and people learn that as infants, but names are usually unique only within a local domain, and it is extremely unlikely that the name by which we know someone would function as a unique identifier on the Internet. In the late 1990s, with the explosion of the Internet, it is likely that one will encounter keyholders who are complete strangers and will remain so, so on first encounter there is no body of knowledge to be indexed by any identifier. The RFC considers building a global database of facts about all persons in the world and making it available, perhaps for a fee, but says that solution would constitute a massive privacy violation and would probably be rejected as politically impossible. Where globally unique identifiers need to be used, the RFC says the best ID is one that is uniform in appearance, such as a long number or random looking text string, so that it has no recognizable sub-field, and large enough that typographical errors would not yield another valid identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The first certificates said who a key belonged to. This section argues that the job of a certificate is better understood as saying what a key is allowed to do, and that names are too weak a base to build on.

sections.title: Authorization Rather Than Authentication
sections.content:
Fully qualified SDSI names represent globally unique names, but at every step of their construction the local name used is presumably meaningful to the issuer. What an application needs to do, when given a public key certificate or a set of them, is answer the question of whether the remote keyholder is permitted some access, and the data needed for that decision is almost never the spelling of a keyholder's name. Instead, the application needs to know if the keyholder is authorized for some access. The RFC states that this is the primary job of a certificate according to the members of the SPKI Working Group, and that the SPKI certificate was designed to meet this need as simply and directly as possible.

Because the world is not going to switch to SPKI certificates overnight, an authorization computation process was developed that can use certificates in any format. The various methods of establishing authorization are documented briefly.

An attribute certificate, as defined in X9.57, binds an attribute that could be an authorization to a Distinguished Name. For an application to use this information it must combine an attribute certificate with an ID certificate to get the full mapping from authorization to name to key. Presumably the two certificates came from different issuers, one an authority on the authorization and the other an authority on names. If either of these issuers were subverted, an attacker could obtain an authorization improperly, so both issuers need to be trusted with the authorization decision.

X.509v3 permits general extensions, which can be used to carry authorization information. This makes the certificate an instrument mapping both authorization to key and name to key, and in this case there is only one issuer, who must be an authority on both the authorization and the name. Some propose issuing a master X.509v3 certificate to an individual and letting extensions hold all the attributes or authorizations the individual would need. That would require the issuer to be an authority on all of those authorizations, and the aggregation of attributes would shorten the lifetime of the certificate, since each attribute would have its own lifetime. Aggregation also amounts to building a dossier and represents a potential privacy violation. For all of these reasons it is desirable that authorizations be limited to one per certificate.

A basic SPKI certificate defines a straight authorization mapping from authorization to key. If someone wants access to a keyholder's name, for logging purposes or for punishment after wrongdoing, the mapping from key to location information gives authorization to key to name. This mapping has an apparent security advantage: only the authorization to key mapping needs to be secure at the level required for the access control mechanism, while the key to name mapping and the issuer of any certificates involved need only be secure enough to satisfy lawyers or private investigators, so a subversion of that mapping does not permit the attacker to defeat the access control. It is also possible that the mapping to name need not be on-line or protected as certificates, since it would be used by human investigators only in unusual circumstances.

SDSI 1.0 defined an ACL granting authorization to names. It was then like an attribute certificate, except that it did not need to be signed or issued by any key: it was held in local memory and was assumed issued by the owner of the computer and therefore of the resource being controlled. In SPKI an ACL entry is free to be implemented in any way the developer chooses, since it is never communicated and does not need to be standardised, although a sample implementation is documented as a certificate body minus the issuer field. The ACL entry can have a name as a subject, as in SDSI 1.0, or it can have a key as a subject. Examples of the latter include the list of SSL root keys in an SSL capable browser, or the file .ssh/authorized_keys in a user's home UNIX directory. Those ACLs are single-purpose, so the individual entries do not carry explicit authorizations, but SPKI uses explicit authorizations so that common authorization computation code can deal with multiple applications.
sections.plainLanguage: There are several ways to write down that a key may do something. The one SPKI prefers ties the authorization straight to the key, so that only one signer has to be trusted.

sections.title: Delegation
sections.content:
One of the powers of an authorization certificate is the ability to delegate authorizations from one person to another without bothering the owner of the resources involved. One might issue a simple permission, for example to read some file, or issue the permission to delegate that permission further. Two issues arose as the authors considered delegation: the desire to limit depth of delegation, and the question of separating delegators from those who can exercise the delegated permission.

On depth there were three camps: no control, boolean control and integer control, and a decision was reached in favour of boolean control. The argument for no control is that if a keyholder is given permission to do something but not permission to delegate it, then it is possible for that keyholder to loan out the empowered private key or set up a proxy service, signing challenges or requests for the intended delegate, so the attempt to restrict delegation is ineffective and might backfire by leading to improper security practices. The argument for boolean control is that one might need to specify an inability to delegate: the RFC imagines the US Commerce Department having a key authorized to declare a cryptographic software module exportable and also to delegate that authorization to manufacturers, and it is reasonable to assume it would not issue permission to delegate further, since it would want a direct legal agreement with each manufacturer. The argument for integer control is that one might want to restrict the depth of delegation to control the proliferation of a delegated permission.

The group chose boolean control. The subject of a certificate or ACL entry may exercise any permission granted and, if delegation is TRUE, may also delegate that permission or a subset of it to others. The no control argument has logical appeal, but there remains the assumption that a user will value his or her private key enough not to loan it out, or that the key will be locked in hardware where it cannot be copied. The integer control option was the original design and has appeal, but was defeated by the inability to predict the proper depth of delegation: one can always need to go one more level down, by creating a temporary signing key, for example for use in a laptop, so the initially predicted depth could be significantly off. And since there is no control on the width of the delegation tree, control on its depth is not a tight control on proliferation.

On whether a delegator may also exercise the permission, the decision was that a delegator is free to create a new key pair, also controlled by it, and delegate the rights to that key to exercise the delegated permission. There was therefore no benefit from attempting to restrict the exercise of a permission by someone permitted to delegate it.

The RFC then compares delegated authorization with traditional authorization-to-name ACLs and name-to-key ID certificates defining groups, and argues the difference with an example. Imagine a firewall proxy permitting telnet and ftp access from the Internet into a network of US Department of Defense machines, where strong access control is desired. Public key authentication and public key certificates could establish who the individual keyholder was, with the private key and the certificates kept on a Fortezza card holding X.509v1 certificates, so all that can be established is the name of the keyholder. It is then the job of the firewall to keep an ACL listing named keyholders and the forms of access each is permitted.

That ACL would not only be potentially huge, demanding far more storage than the firewall would otherwise require, but it would also need its own ACL. One could not, for example, have someone in the Army decide whether someone in the Navy got access; the ACL would probably need a nested set of ACLs, eventually reflecting the organisation structure of the entire Defense Department. Without the ACLs the firewall could be a device with no mass storage, small enough to hold in one hand; with them it would need a large storage device accessed both for making access control decisions and for updating the ACLs.

By contrast, let the access be controlled by authorization certificates. The firewall would have an ACL with one entry, granting a key belonging to the Secretary of Defense the right to delegate all access through the firewall. The Secretary would then issue certificates delegating the permission to delegate to each of their subordinates, and this process would iterate until some enlisted man received permission to penetrate that firewall for one specific protocol but not the permission to delegate it. The certificate structure generated would reflect the organisation structure of the entire Department, just as the nested ACLs would, but the control of these certificates, through their issuance and revocation, is distributed and need not show up in that one firewall or be replicated in all firewalls.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate can pass its permission on to someone else. The RFC decides that this is controlled by one yes-or-no flag rather than by a count, and argues that passing permissions along through certificates is much easier to run than keeping one enormous list at the firewall.

sections.title: The 5-Tuple and Its Reduction
sections.content:
The 5-tuple is an intermediate form, assumed to be held in trusted memory so that it does not need a digital signature for integrity. It is produced from certificates or other credentials via trusted software. Its contents are the same as the contents of an SPKI certificate body, but it might be derived from another form of certificate or from an ACL entry.

The elements of a 5-tuple are five. The Issuer is a public key, or its hash, or the reserved word Self, and identifies the entity speaking this intermediate result. The Subject is a public key or its hash, a name used to identify a public key, the hash of an object, or a threshold function of subordinate subjects, and identifies the entity being spoken about. Delegation is a boolean: if TRUE, the Subject is permitted by the Issuer to further propagate the authorization. Authorization is an S-expression, a list of strings or sub-lists whose meaning is to and probably defined by the application that will use the authorization for access control. Validity dates are a not-before date and a not-after date, where date means date and time; if the not-before date is missing from the source credential then minus infinity is assumed, and if the not-after date is missing then plus infinity is assumed.

A name-to-key certificate, such as X.509v1 or SDSI 1.0, carries no authorization field but does carry a name, and since it is qualitatively different from an authorization certificate a separate intermediate form is defined for it. The elements of a name 4-tuple are the Issuer, a public key or its hash, identifying the entity defining this name in its private name space; the Name, a byte string; the Subject, a public key or its hash, a name, or a threshold function of subordinate subjects, which defines the name; and the Validity dates, with the same rules about missing dates.

The reduction rule for two 5-tuples, written as issuer, subject, delegation, authorization and validity, is that two tuples yield one tuple with the first issuer, the second subject, the second delegation, the intersection of the two authorizations and the intersection of the two validity intervals, provided the two intersections succeed, the first subject equals the second issuer, and the first delegation is TRUE.

Two authorizations intersect by matching element for element. If one list is longer than the other but they match at all elements where both have elements, the longer list is the result of the intersection, which means that additional elements of a list must restrict the permission granted. The RFC gives the example of an ftpd that allows public key access control using authorization certificates, where (ftp (host ftp.clark.net)) might imply that the keyholder is allowed ftp access to all directories on that host with all kinds of access, which is more general than (ftp (host ftp.clark.net) (dir /pub/cme)), which allows all kinds of access but only in the directory specified. The intersection of the two is the second.
sections.plainLanguage: To answer the question, the software turns every certificate into the same five-part shape and then joins two of them up. Two results can be joined only when the first one's subject is the second one's issuer and the first one allows further delegation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are three classes of information that can be bound together by public key certificates: key, name and authorization. There are therefore three general kinds of certificate, depending on what pair of items the certificate ties together, and considering the direction of mapping there are six classes: name to key, key to name, authorization to name, name to authorization, authorization to key, and key to authorization.

The SPKI working group concluded that the most important use for certificates was access control. Given the various kinds of mapping possible, there are at least two ways to implement access control. One can use a straight authorization certificate mapping an authorization to a key, or one can use an attribute certificate and an ID certificate, mapping an authorization to a name and then a name to a key.

There are at least two ways in which the former is more secure than the latter. Each certificate has an issuer, and if that issuer is subverted then the attacker can gain access: in the former case there is only one issuer to trust, while in the latter there are two. And in the second case the linkage between the certificates is by name. If the name space of the issuer of the ID certificate is different from the name space of the issuer of the attribute certificate, then one of the two issuers must use a foreign name space, and the process of choosing the appropriate name from a foreign name space is more complex than string matching and might even involve a human guess. It is subject to mistakes, and such a mistake can be made by accident or be guided by an attacker.

The RFC says this is not to say that one must never use the second construct, since if the two certificates come from the same issuer, and therefore with the same name space, then both of the security differentiators are cancelled out.
sections.plainLanguage: Tying the permission straight to the key means one signer to trust and no name matching to get wrong. Splitting it across two certificates means two signers and a name that has to line up.
